On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya commands Sitaram and threatens to fight him. Sitaram, grateful that the prince has twice saved his life, submits and asks to be disarmed and bound to protect him from the king’s punishment. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, their roles reverse: Sitaram takes charge, opens the prison, and practically carries the prince out, while Udayaditya, weakened and disoriented by confinement, helplessly asks what to do and where to go, relying on Sitaram to guide him.

Pratapaditya first sends two Pathan brothers to murder Basanta Ray on his journey to Jessore, intending to strike at the Simultali inn. One brother lures away his attendants with a false report of a dacoit attack, but the other, moved by Basanta Ray’s kindness, refuses to kill him. Later, Pratapaditya sends Muktiyar Khan with a signed death order and soldiers who infiltrate Raigarh in disguise. Abdul finally kills Basanta Ray with a sword while the old king prays before his deity.

In the Mahishi’s room within Jessore’s inner quarters, Ramai is disguised as a middle-aged woman; Rammohan seizes, swings, chokes, and carries him away tied in a shawl. In Ramchandra Ray’s palace room in Chandradwip, Ramai appears as himself, the court jester, without a disguise; after he insults Vibha, Rammohan grabs him by the scruff and throws him out.
Rukmini, disguised as Mangala, secretly prepares poison disguised as medicine requested by the Mahishi through Matangini. This poisoning kills Surma before her planned exile.

Her refusal wounds Ramchandra Ray’s pride, prompting him to marry another woman in revenge. When Vibha finally reaches Chandradwip, she discovers that her husband is marrying that very day and that she no longer has a place in his palace, shattering her hopes of happiness.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya’s signet ring by demanding it when he offers her anything to keep her away from Surma’s bed. Sitaram and Bhagavat then use its engraved seal to authenticate a forged petition, supposedly from Udayaditya to the Emperor, accusing Pratapaditya of treason and seeking the kingdom for himself. Instead of taking it to Delhi, Bhagavat gives it to Pratapaditya, falsely claiming he intercepted it from Udayaditya’s servant. Pratapaditya uses the petition as a pretext to imprison Udayaditya, despite admitting that he does not particularly believe the accusation.

Udayaditya’s role in Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape led to the dismissal of the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat and brought him under Pratapaditya’s closer scrutiny. Feeling responsible for their families’ hardship, Udayaditya gave them monthly stipends. Pratapaditya regarded this charity as defiance of his punishment and expressly forbade further help. Surma then secretly continued the payments through a trusted maid, who disclosed the arrangement to Mangala. When Pratapaditya learned of it, he ordered Surma sent to her paternal home. Her initial refusal ultimately prompted him to threaten Udayaditya with imprisonment, forcing her to agree to leave.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness, grief, and sense of emptiness after losing the companionship of loved ones. He first sings it alone at sunset in Raigarh, wistfully remembering those who once shared his joy. Later, he sings it while holding Vibha’s hand outside Surma’s silent, empty room in Jessore, where his private longing becomes shared grief over the family’s desolation.

After failing to stop Udayaditya’s escape, Rukmini survives her plunge into the canal and exposes the escape to Pratapaditya, accusing Basanta Ray, Udayaditya, and Sitaram of conspiring together. Her report destroys the deception that Udayaditya died in the fire, and men sent with her confirm that he is in Raigarh. Pratapaditya then sends Muktiyar Khan with orders to capture Udayaditya and execute Basanta Ray. Rukmini helps the soldiers locate Udayaditya, whose capture prevents him from warning or defending his grand-uncle. Muktiyar refuses Udayaditya’s pleas and has Abdul kill Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya initially treats Ramchandra with cool indifference, offering little ceremonial welcome and prioritizing official business over their conversation, making Ramchandra feel inferior. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra reverses this hierarchy by encouraging ridicule of Pratapaditya’s ancestry and royal standing, asserting his own family’s superiority, and treating his marriage to Pratapaditya’s daughter as an honor bestowed on an inferior house.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore. Hoping to control Udayaditya’s heart and eventually his kingdom, she befriends palace servants and monitors palace affairs. When the queen secretly seeks medicine to turn Udayaditya away from Surma, Rukmini supplies poison disguised as that medicine, leading to Surma’s death. Later, she enters the grieving prince’s room, manipulates his guilt over their past, demands his love, and leaves with his ring when he refuses to let her approach Surma’s bed.

Udayaditya initially wishes he had never been born crown prince, believing that royal life has brought him scrutiny, paternal contempt, and unhappiness rather than affection. His desire to escape this burden becomes decisive after his grand-uncle’s murder, when he despairs that his weakness has brought ruin upon others. Brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he asks to be released from the throne and names Samaraditya as heir. He then formally swears before Ma-Kali, in his father’s presence, never to claim any part of Jessore’s kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its royal scepter, invoking the guilt of his grand-uncle’s murder if he breaks the oath. With Pratapaditya’s consent, he prepares to leave for Kashi, where he intends to establish a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle’s memory.

After Rammohan refuses to carry Ramchandra Ray’s letter renouncing Vibha, it is entrusted to Nayanchand. Fearing Pratapaditya’s reaction, Nayanchand delivers it to the Mahishi instead. She conceals its contents from both Pratapaditya and Vibha, then shows it to Basanta Ray. Believing Ramchandra wrote only in anger and would relent if Vibha returned, Basanta advises her to announce that the letter requests Vibha’s return to Chandradwip. The Mahishi repeats this false account to Vibha and the household, leading Vibha to believe her husband has understood and forgiven her and lovingly sent for her.

Pratapaditya tries to trap Ramchandra by locking the palace exits and blocking the adjoining canal with large sal logs. Udayaditya overcomes the guards, and Rammohan lowers Ramchandra from the roof into his boat using a rope made of sheets. When the boat reaches the blockade, Rammohan and his men haul it over the logs. The guards’ stones fall short, their firearm preparations are confused, and their pursuit boat arrives too late, allowing Ramchandra to reach the Bhairav River.

Basanta Ray’s sitar, once his constant companion, becomes a symbol of joy destroyed by separation from Udayaditya. At their farewell, he plays furiously to contain his grief, but tears and a choked throat force him to stop. He leaves the instrument behind, declaring that he will never play it again. Later, his remark that its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned mirrors his own wounded heart: music remains, but its joy has vanished without his loved ones. When news of Udayaditya’s imprisonment abruptly silences his briefly revived singing, it shows how completely his happiness depends on Udayaditya’s well-being.

Earlier, Udayaditya courageously defended oppressed subjects, defying his father’s wishes and intervening without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, grief and an overwhelming fear of Pratapaditya undermine his courage. Though he still feels compassion and intends to help, he retreats from stopping violence, abandons plans to prevent looting, and fails to send financial aid.

Sitaram undoes his role in causing Udayaditya’s imprisonment through the forged petition by rescuing him. During the fire, he enters the prison, pulls Udayaditya out, and leads him away, having first brought Basanta Ray out of the palace to help with the escape.

First, Rammohan carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down a rope made from thick sheets tied to a palace-roof pillar. At the rope’s end, he grips it with his teeth, carefully lowers the king into the boat with both hands, and jumps aboard himself. He and his followers then haul the boat over logs blocking the canal.

Later, after Vibha is rejected and faints in Ramchandra’s palace, Rammohan lifts her, carries her outside, places her in a palanquin near the gate, and takes her back to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately adorned by her mother with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an imposing coiffure. Despite discomfort with these ornaments, her face radiates shy joy at her husband’s arrival. In Chandradwip, she dresses as a common woman, rejects a palanquin, and approaches him like a subject or beggar. Veiled, tearful, and without any royal welcome, she falls at his feet—and he mistakes her for a beggar seeking alms. Her presentation shifts from lavish royal splendor and joyful anticipation to plainness, grief, and humiliation.

In his bedchamber, the window symbolizes grief and longing: its familiar view recalls his life with Surma, and he returns to it hoping to find her in her usual place. In prison, the window becomes a source of hope and inner freedom. The sky and flying birds remind him that his confinement may end and that, despite the king’s power, his spirit is naturally free. Its meaning shifts from attachment to an irretrievable past to the possibility of future liberation.

Initially, the penniless Sitaram courts Rukmini for both her beauty and her money. She lends him cash while encouraging affectionate banter, and he neglects repayment as their frequent meetings develop into secret plotting.

Their relationship breaks down when Udayaditya is imprisoned. Sitaram blames Rukmini, curses her, threatens to burn her house and publicly humiliate her, and vows to free the prince. Rukmini responds with furious possessiveness, insisting that only she has the right to help or harm Udayaditya.

After arranging Udayaditya’s escape and staging his death in a fire, Sitaram visits Rukmini’s house to steal her money, believing her dead. Finding her alive, he first mocks her, then tries to revive their old flirtation. But her shattered hopes and rage make his false affection intolerable. She threatens to kill both him and Udayaditya and fetches a curved blade. Sitaram escapes before she returns and strikes the floor where he stood. Realizing she can expose his scheme, he regrets not strangling her and immediately flees Jessore with his family.

Sitaram first arranges fires in the guards’ quarters to draw them away from Udayaditya’s prison, exploiting their concern for their belongings. He then brings Udayaditya out under the pretext that the prison is on fire and helps him escape with Basanta Ray. His accomplices prolong the distraction by sabotaging firefighting efforts.

The scheme becomes a cover-up when they deliberately burn the now-empty prison cell. Returning after Udayaditya’s boat reaches the river, Sitaram plants bones, a skull, and the prince’s sword inside. Reports of screams, followed by Sitaram’s announcement that the roof has collapsed and Udayaditya no longer responds, create the impression that the prince died in the blaze. He also retrieves Udayaditya’s letters and destroys one, further controlling evidence of the escape. The apparent death is supported by supposed eyewitness testimony and the burned sword, buying time until Rukmini exposes the plot and later reports confirm Udayaditya is alive.

Ramchandra Ray treats Udayaditya’s rescue as an obligation rather than a kindness, believing he acted chiefly to protect his sister, not to save Ramchandra’s life. Ungrateful, he joins his courtiers in mocking Udayaditya simply for being Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya initially dismisses the Emperor’s displeasure as an “empty fear,” insisting that Delhi has no authority over him, yet already suspects Udayaditya of lodging a complaint there. Bhagavat and Sitaram exploit this suspicion by forging a petition, stamped with the prince’s seal, accusing Pratapaditya of treason and seeking the kingdom for Udayaditya. Instead of delivering it to Delhi, Bhagavat gives it to Pratapaditya, claiming to have intercepted it from the prince’s servant. Thus, the imperial threat Pratapaditya scorns becomes fabricated evidence of his son’s betrayal, providing the pretext for imprisoning him.

Vibha’s hair makes Surma’s loving presence—and later her absence—visible. In Chapter 8, Vibha secretly turns to Surma to restyle her hair according to her own taste, revealing their intimacy and Surma’s understanding, in contrast to the Mahishi’s imposed adornment and accusations of jealousy. After Surma is gone, Vibha sits waiting for her to braid it, but evening passes and her hair remains unbraided. The interrupted ritual expresses both her disbelief and the loss of Surma’s comforting care. By Chapter 23, Rammohan notices her unkempt hair as evidence that no one cares for her: what once marked affectionate companionship now marks grief, neglect, and loneliness within the palace.
